title: Continuum mechanics
description: Branch of physics which studies the behavior of materials modeled as continuous media
wiki_lead:
Continuum mechanics is a branch of mechanics that deals with the deformation of and transmission of forces through materials modeled as a continuous medium (also called a continuum) rather than as discrete particles. 
Continuum mechanics deals with deformable bodies, as opposed to rigid bodies. 
A continuum model assumes that the substance of the object completely fills the space it occupies. While ignoring the fact that matter is made of atoms, this provides a sufficiently accurate description of matter on length scales much greater than that of inter-atomic distances. The concept of a continuous medium allows for intuitive analysis of bulk matter by using differential equations that describe the behavior of such matter according to physical laws, such as mass conservation, momentum conservation, and energy conservation. Information about the specific material is expressed in constitutive relationships.
Continuum mechanics treats the physical properties of solids and fluids independently of any particular coordinate system in which they are observed. These properties are represented by tensors, which are mathematical objects with the salient property of being independent of coordinate systems. This permits definition of physical properties at any point in the continuum, according to mathematically convenient continuous functions. The theories of elasticity, plasticity and fluid mechanics are based on the concepts of continuum mechanics.

Continuum mechanics treats the physical properties of solids and fluids independently of any particular coordinate system in which they are observed. These properties are represented by tensors, which are mathematical objects with the salient property of being independent of coordinate systems. This permits definition of physical properties at any point in the continuum, according to mathematically convenient continuous functions. The theories of elasticity, plasticity and fluid mechanics are based on the concepts of continuum mechanics.


Concept of a continuum
The concept of a continuum underlies the mathematical framework for studying large-scale forces and deformations in materials. Although materials are composed of discrete atoms and molecules, separated by empty space or microscopic cracks and crystallographic defects, physical phenomena can often be modeled by considering a substance distributed throughout some region of space. A continuum is a body that can be continually sub-divided into infinitesimal elements with local material properties defined at any particular point. Properties of the bulk material can therefore be described by almost everywhere smooth functions of position in the continuum, and their evolution with time can be studied using calculus.
Apart from the assumption of continuity, two other independent assumptions are often employed in the study of continuum mechanics. These are homogeneity (assumption of identical properties at all locations) and isotropy (assumption of directionally invariant vector properties). If these auxiliary assumptions are not globally applicable, the material may be segregated into sections where they are applicable in order to simplify the analysis. For more complex cases, one or both of these assumptions can be dropped. In these cases, computational methods are often used to solve the differential equations describing the evolution of material properties.


Major areas

An additional area of continuum mechanics comprises elastomeric foams, which exhibit a curious hyperbolic stress-strain relationship.  The elastomer is a true continuum, but a homogeneous distribution of voids gives it unusual properties.


Formulation of models

Continuum mechanics models begin by assigning a region in three-dimensional Euclidean space to the material body ℬ being modeled. The points within this region are called particles or material points. Different configurations or states of the body correspond to different regions in Euclidean space. grok_lead: Continuum mechanics is a foundational branch of classical mechanics and applied mathematics that treats materialsâsuch as solids, fluids, and gasesâas continuous media rather than discrete collections of atoms or molecules, enabling the analysis of deformation, motion, stress, and energy transfer at macroscopic scales where atomic structures can be neglected. This approach assumes matter is infinitely divisible and locally homogeneous, with physical properties like density, velocity, and stress represented as smooth, continuous fields that vary smoothly in space and time, valid for length scales much larger than atomic spacings (on the order of 10^{-10} m) and time scales longer than molecular vibrations (around 10^{-15} s). The field encompasses the kinematics of material deformationâdescribing how bodies change shape and position through mappings from reference to current configurationsâand the dynamics governed by fundamental balance laws for mass, linear momentum, angular momentum, energy, and entropy. These laws, often expressed as partial differential equations, are supplemented by constitutive relations that link stress and strain to material -specific responses, such as elasticity in solids or viscosity in fluids, allowing predictions of behavior under diverse loading conditions like tension, shear, or thermal gradients. Descriptions of motion are formulated in either Lagrangian coordinates, which track individual material particles over time, or Eulerian coordinates, which focus on fixed points in space through which material flows. Historically, continuum mechanics traces its origins to ancient approximations by Archimedes and was formalized in the 17th and 18th centuries through Isaac Newton's laws of motion and Leonhard Euler's contributions to fluid dynamics, with pivotal 19th-century advancements by Augustin-Louis Cauchy in stress tensor theory and Jean-Marie Constant Duhamel in thermoelasticity. The 20th century saw a renaissance, driven by figures like Clifford Truesdell and Walter Noll, who developed rigorous axiomatic frameworks integrating nonlinear effects and thermodynamics, enabling applications in complex phenomena such as viscoelasticity, plasticity, and shock wave propagation. Key applications span engineering disciplines, including structural analysis of deformable solids, aerodynamics and hydrodynamics for fluid flows, geophysics for tectonic deformations, and biomechanics for soft tissues, often leveraging computational methods to solve nonlinear problems intractable analytically. Mathematical tools central to the field include tensor calculus for invariant representations of stress and strain, the deformation gradient tensor to quantify stretches and rotations, and integral theorems like the Reynolds transport theorem for deriving local field equations from global balances. By providing a general, material-independent foundation, continuum mechanics unifies disparate theories like elasticity and fluid dynamics while accommodating specialized extensions, such as thermoelasticity or models for anisotropic materials like liquid crystals.
